entries.title: The Cult of Khul Anar (the Cythranai)
entries.body:
A people of the island, known to outsiders as raiders. Their warrior culture prizes the coliseums of Khul Anar and the honored rage-riders who return from the hunt on pale rage-stags.

The cult's seat is home of its coliseums, where champions are proven in the pits.

entries.title: The Twin Spirits
entries.body: The name outsiders give the two apex spirits of the island, so-called for being ever-together. To the peoples beyond, they are the guardians and terrors of that place.

entries.title: Caerwynne
entries.body: Holds two titles at once: Marshall of the Cult of Khul Anar and Grand Gladiatrix, champion of the coliseums. The Gladiatrix crown is won like a title belt; few climb high enough to challenge her.

entries.title: Sontrailles
entries.body: The Marches of Sontrailles is a realm nestled within the northern Border Princes region, situated among the Geistenmund Hills. Its namesake city is heavily fortified and serves as the heart of the region with both inner and outer walls bristling with cannons. It is encircled by many hamlets and villages, with the foremost settlements being the key towns of Roucourt, Cervelliers, Coutenagne, Fleurois, and Verois. In the valley below, agriculture thrives on fertile soil, where peasants toil from before the sun rises to long after it sets, tending crops for their liege lords. Their labors are but a pittance tax, paid in full for the blood spilt by their betters in defense of the realm. Every Spring until Autumn the grass in the region turns a vibrant flaming red and in the winter the grass turns purple. In the Geistenmund hills themselves silver and other valuable ores are extracted by miners who risk their very lives in the dark tunnels often infested with ratmen and “others” as the Sontraillais would call them. The realm’s goods flow from the hands of skilled artisans, their craft tightly controlled by the guilds, whose prices and production are regularly negotiated with the nobility. Workshops forge tools, weapons, and armor, while merchants ferry goods to the surrounding towns, connecting the scattered settlements into the economy. In the days of Charlen’s Crusade it was one of many castles raised as a bulwark against the ork tides by Etienne de Chatlon of Moussillon. There behind its high walls the desperate and weary found safety and knights found brief respite before rallying again to face the unending green tides. More than a century has passed since its founding, it is the nucleus of a small realm within the Border Princes. In the wake of Tamurkhan’s march on the Empire the survivors of the crusader realm clustered to its walls, once again raising their banners and growing a nation from the stitched corpses of the old bretonnian fiefs. Though nominally a member of the Northern Border Confederacy, Sontrailles and its neighboring settlements have a long and storied history of both unity and conflict. While they have stood together against dastard threats such as the Dawi Zharr, savage Beastmen, druchii, and marauding Greenskins, they have just as often turned their spears upon one another in bitter feuds. In more recent times, a newly ratified treaty has again secured Sontrailles’ place within the confederacy. With the current marquis maintaining close ties with the lords of Krenhalften and Akendorf, there is cautious optimism among the common folk. Many dare to hope that for a few seasons diplomacy will hold, and the fragile alliance will not dissolve into yet another cycle of bloodshed. While Akendorf and Krenhalften are among the closest allies of Sontrailles, its greatest trade ally lies across the Southern Sea in Araby. All year round merchants from Sontrailles travel to Araby to bring back exotic goods and merchants from Araby maintain their own quarter in the town of Flumontel, ensuring the flow of goods never ceases. It is said that the marquis spent years of his time as the “Wayfaring Knight” in Araby and there in Al Sahrun he fought side by side with the Sultan against vampire lords. History The Founding and Reign of Etienne Sontrailles A stylized drawing of the fortress-city of Sontrailles Heraldry of the Armand De Sontrailles, called “King Death’s Right Hand”, fifth Marquis of Sontrailles Founded 1443 (2421 IC) Type Marquisate Location Geistemund Hills, Badlands, Old World Population Around 40,000 in Sontrailles proper. Inhabitants Humans, Dwarfs, Elves, Gnomes, Giants, Orcs. Ruler Marquis Armand de Sontrailles Major Settlements Roucourt, Cervellier, Coutenagne, Chaufourrier, Flumontel, Brulivaux Industry Finished Silver and Gold Products Wine Liquors Ore and Ingots Agriculture Textiles High Fashion Clothing Arms and Armor Glass “..I leave the legacy of our people to you, shall the strength of our lances never fail...” - Last words of Etienne de Chatlon, as recorded by historian Rolin of Sontrailles Over a century ago in the defunct dukedom of Mousillon, Sir Etienne de Chatlon was sworn to defend a remote fiefdom under the rule of his liege lord, the Baron of Aubagne-sur-Grismerie. It was there in the misty swamps that he spent the early years of his knighthood. His days were consumed by an endless battle against lurking mutants, ghouls, and occasional beastman. The work was grueling and unrelenting, yet he was not alone. The men-at-arms under his command were few yet they made up for their small numbers with valor. It is said that Etienne’s weary heart found a quiet joy in the form of the mercer’s daughter who would bring warm meals to him in his humble keep. Together they dreamt of a fief of their own but their time together was cruelly short and soon she was taken by pox. For years Etienne took to drinking, rarely leaving the village tower unless roused by his men. In 2420, when King Charlen issued his doomed decree for an errantry war, he extended the call to arms even to the knights of disgraced Mousillon, allowing them the chance to march to the aid of the Border Princes. Sir Etienne de Chatlon believed this was a sign sent from the Lady and an opportunity to leave the cursed swamps and carve a realm out in her name and acted with vigor unseen in years. With his liege lord’s blessing he gathered a host of knights, men at arms, and peasants who, though humble in station, sought to escape the horrors of the blighted marshes.Only those deemed wholesome in form were permitted to march, for this was to be a noble endeavor, free of the taint that had long plagued Mousillon. As soon as Etienne crossed the Grismerie, errant knights flocked to his banner, drawn by the promise of battle and renown. Exiled and disgraced knights cast from their homes and stripped of their honors likewise sought him out, clinging to the forlorn hope that by answering Royarch’s call they might one day reclaim their lost prestige.The road was perilous, yet the campaign was rich with glory. Victory followed victory, and all who dared oppose their march were crushed beneath their hooves. None would bar their path to the Border Princes. It was during these arduous marches that a band of traveling priests of Morr, led by a devout cleric named Siegert who claimed to be a dreamwalker, approached the host. They beseeched Etienne for leave to accompany his force, convinced that a great battle against the enemies of their patron whom they named King Death lay ahead. When he allowed them into his warband they blessed his lance, calling upon Morr to guide it true in the battles to come.These priests took upon themselves the solemn duty of consecrating the fallen after each engagement, ensuring the dead were granted the proper rites before passing into the next world. However, among the ranks, discontent simmered. Many of the young and impetuous knights grew impatient with the delays, resentful of being slowed by the followers of a lesser god. Yet, Etienne would not deny brave souls their final honors. He decreed that the priests be allowed to carry out their sacred work, though with a greater sense of urgency to keep the march from faltering. When at last the Bretonnians met the oncoming tide of greenskins east of the Appucini Mountains, the battlefield became a proving ground for righteous steel. The warbosses, in their brutish arrogance, believed sheer numbers would overcome chivalric might. They were sorely mistaken. Against the charge of noble lances and the implacable wall of shields, the greenskin hordes broke like waves upon an unshakeable cliff. Time and again their leaders fell, heads cloven and hearts pierced, until at last their armies lay shattered and the land was strewn with the carcasses of the vanquished. The fleeing greenskins were pursued without mercy to the river, where they were cut down to the last miserable grot. Such was the carnage that the waters themselves ran red with ork blood, and henceforth it was known as the Blood River. Blood river was as far east as Etienne brought his army however. It was not long before the greenskins returned with greater numbers and long gone were the swift victories of the crusaders. Now a war of grinding attrition began. With the crusade stalled Etienne sought ground that could be held against the hordes. Scouts scoured the surrounding lands and they reported that the Geistenmund hills could hold a fortress. It was a rugged line of stone with few arable slopes and broken ridges overlooking the valley. There he ordered the construction of a great fortress, one that could anchor the crusader host and stand as a bulwark against the green tide. Locals told tales of necromancers from olden days fleeing from the west and claiming the hills for their own and raising undead servants. The priests of Morr knew now why their dreamwalker was led to the crusaders. Stone was quarried from the hills themselves, timber dragged from distant forests, and with urgency the first palisades rose. The fortress was raised under ceaseless threat. Greenskin warbands assaulted the builders day and night, while from the hills and old burial grounds the restless dead clawed their way to the surface and beastmen were drawn in from the sounds of the chisels and war. Laborers worked with weapons close at hand, and many times unfinished walls ran slick with blood before the mortar had fully set. Knights and men-at-arms stood watch from makeshift ramparts, beating back assaults while masons laid stone behind them. Amidst this turmoil, the priests of Morr labored as tirelessly as any mason. Siegert conducted the sanctification rites in concert with his brethren, consecrating the earth and sealing ancient graves with wards. Funerary bells tolled at dusk and dawn, and black robed figures traced sigils of rest into the bedrock itself. Where their rites took hold, the dead grew still, and the land, long profaned by dark magics, were purified. Some practitioners of dark magic rose to challenge the crusaders, unleashing hordes of zombies and unwilling to relinquish their grip upon the hills. Etienne and his knights crashed into the wall of decaying flesh, and it is said that in the first charge alone he skewered five corpses upon his lance. The charnel guard could not bar the knights from their prey, and the coven of necromancers was cut down, their deaths breaking the sorcery that bound the dead to their will. Freed from enchantment, the zombies collapsed into lifeless ruin. Word of the victory spread swiftly and the displaced and desperate made their way toward the Geistenmund Hills, drawn by the promise of safety behind the rising walls. The threat however, was not eliminated and the denizens of the night continued their assault in the night. The loquacious simple folk whispered of a great lich lurking still in the hills, or even worse, heading to them. Etienne himself could not always take up the banner in defense, and so he appointed two stalwart commanders to command in his stead. By day, Ramnulf de Naizon held the line, rallying his warriors to deeds of valor against vile greenskins and loathsome beastmen, driving them back into the wretched dens from whence they came. By night, however, vengeful spirits and ghastly horrors assailed the fortified positions, summoned forth by the will of NIGHT’S DARK MASTERS. Against these terrors stood the men under the command of Aedric d’Aubagne, a knight of storied bloodline who traced his lineage to a paladin in service of the great Landuin himself. Thus it was recorded that, in this grim theater of war, the priests of Morr proved indispensable. When dusk fell, they gathered the warriors beneath the darkening sky and set their sacred offices to work, laying blessings upon man and steel alike. By these rites were hearts made steadfast and weapons hallowed, so that those who marched forth might strike the unholy with righteous purpose It is written, “..with longsword wielded two handed, Aedric strode into the darkness at the head of his men, and where his blade fell, the gibbering fiends were sundered as though night itself had been cut apart. It was said that no shadow could cling where he stood, and that each stroke scattered them from his gaze. From dusk until dawn the priests labored without rest, consecrating the earth about the fortress, and with each passing night they followed in his wake, pressing ever farther into the cursed lands. Thus were the foul sorceries unraveled, and thus was the grip of the dead loosened, until the darkness itself seemed to recoil from their advance.” As the castle neared completion, a dread host fell upon the Bretonnian lines, a lance of red armored knights riding at the fore of a seething tide of ghouls and shambling corpses numbering in the thousands and broke through the outer defenses. When Aedric returned with the few who yet survived, bearing word of their approach, final preparations were made in haste.By the time the dead dragged themselves to the foot of the hills, all within the castle stood ready. At Etienne’s command, volleys of flaming arrows arced into the night, and the great engines of war loosed their wrath upon the ravening horde. Missiles tore through rotting flesh and shattered rusted mail, yet still the undead advanced as one relentless mass flesh heedless of pain, clawing ever closer to the unfinished walls.Then the dead hurled themselves upon the defenders with reckless fury and high upon his shadowed perch, the lich lord cast forth vile hexes and blighting curses, his foul sorcery seeking to unmake the courage of the living. Yet the defenders did not falter. With grim resolve they reinforced the gaps with sharpened stakes and deep dug trenches, hardening their line even as the assault fell upon them. Thus were the oncoming masses funneled into narrow columns, where each wave of the undead met a concentrated wall of steel and missile fire. There their numbers were ground away, shattered into the maw of the castle’s fortifications. The bellicose knights who were used to fighting mounted were held in check by Etienne’s measured command and fought on foot. He would not allow them to overextend beyond the shelter of the walls, for he knew well that such valor, loosed too soon, would invite only ruin. It was by the power of the assembled conclave that the malignant sorcery of the lich was gatehouse at last countered, though not without grievous cost. In one of the shattered gaps in the line stood Etienne himself. His blessed blade burned brightly in the night, hewing down crypt horrors and cairn wraiths. Yet even he, strong of will though he was, remained but mortal. Wound upon wound was laid upon him, and still he would not yield. Though his men begged him to withdraw to safety, his resolve did not break. He would not forsake his duty nor abandon the line. Shoulder to shoulder with his warriors he stood, the roar of battle rolling across the hills, his sword rising and falling without falter as the dead continued unrelenting. Then the dark knights charged at full tilt, their cursed steeds thundering over the earth, smashing aside all who dared stand before them. Among their number rode one clad in tarnished red-gold armor, who at the height of the assault reined in his nightmarish mount and dismounted. From its scabbard he drew a blade etched with dark runes, and upon his shield was a faded fleur-de-lys, its colors long since stained and dulled. He cut down all who barred his path, yet there was something unsettling in his method. He did not strike the knights of Bretonnia with the same ruthless abandon he showed the common soldiery. Instead, there was a cruel deliberation to his movements. He toyed with them circling, testing, dancing just beyond their defenses and only when they were spent did he deliver the killing blow. Often he would pause, studying their tabard’s and shield’s heraldry as though committing bloodlines to memory before ending their lives. Seeing the line falter beneath this relentless assault, Etienne moved to meet him, seeking to blunt the creature’s advance. From the first exchange it was clear he was hard-pressed. The dark knight’s movements were swift beyond mortal measure, and Etienne’s blade found no purchase. Whether the foe was simply beyond him, or whether the mounting toll of his wounds had begun to betray him, none could say. No man dared voice the thought aloud, yet the truth was plain to see, Etienne was driven back, step by step, until at last his knee struck the earth. Before the final blow could fall, a familiar voice rang out above the din. Brave Aedric, hacking his way through a tide of ghouls and shambling dead, came to his liege lord’s side, spoke his full name aloud, declaring his lineage and daring the cursed knight to face him. Rolin would write of the duel, “But when the name of Aedric was spoken, the fell knight turned, and the wounded lord was forgotten. A wrath long kindled awoke within him, and he cried aloud, and the sound was as iron riven.Then he came upon Aedric, and their swords were as fire in the gloom. Around them the dark riders stood in silence, and none might pass their guard. Yet though Aedric was valiant and unafraid, his doom was upon him. For the red-gold warrior struck not in sport,his blade was sure. Soon the bright mail of Aedric was darkened with blood, and he fell, and the earth received him. In pride the victor despoiled him and departed into the night, and his brethren with him, and their passing was as a shadow drawn across the field. But when they were gone, the power of the dead waned, and the host of ghouls faltered. Then the living took heart once more, though they were weary unto death; and amid ruin and sorrow there stirred again a small and steadfast hope.” Siegert, leading a valiant band of knights, spearheaded the charge through the relentless tide of the undead to confront the lich. The elderly priest who was made frail by the sands of time faltered beneath the dark magics, his strength waning with each spell and one by one, the knights fell, overwhelmed by the unholy horde. Yet amid the carnage, Sir Vortigern stood, shielded by the divine power. Enduring the dark magics, in the decisive moment he struck the lich down with his ensorcelled blade cutting through the cursed flesh and ending the terror once and for all. As the lich crumbled to dust, disintegrating upon the winds, it unleashed one final, venomous curse, a gale of malevolent energy that reverberated through the land, casting a briefly lingering shadow upon the earth. Though the immediate threat was ended the lingering darkness seeped into the earth. At dawn, the castle stood secure. Over the fortnight that followed, it was completed and named Aedric’s Rest in honor of the knight’s ultimate sacrifice. Etienne took Aedric’s son into his care, raising him in the arts of warfare and ultimately placing him within his retinue when he came of age. Years passed as the castle expanded into a city and it became a safe haven for the crusaders and refugees with its sturdy walls. During its expansion Etienne journeyed to Mousillon personally, where he pledged fealty to both the barony and the royarch Charlen. In recognition of his loyalty, he was granted the title of Marquis by decree of the royarch, allowed to rule his march in service to the baron of Aubagne-sur-Grismerie. The city was named Sontrailles, chosen long ago by Etienne and his paramour for the village they had dreamed to build together. In 2429, Etienne and the other Border Princes marched against the invading armies of Emperor Dieter IV, a campaign cut short by the accession of Wilhelm the Wise. Two years later, in 2431, Sir Etienne was mortally wounded defending the southern gatehouse of Sontrailles during a greenskin assault. It is written by Rolin of Sontrailles that: “Even as his armor ran red with his own lifeblood Etienne stood amidst the greenskins unbowed and unbroken. He struck a mutual killing blow upon the menace warlord and fell upon the mountain of corpses. The gatehouse would not fall that day.” With his final breath, he named Sir Ramnulf as his successor, entrusting him with the city’s protection. Taken into Morr’s embrace, Etienne passed with his legacy secure, the city forever marked by his sacrifice. The gatehouse, by his courage, did not fall that day.

entries.title: Duties Owed unto the Marquis
entries.body:
Duties Owed unto the Marquis

I. Homage and Fealty

Every lord holding land and acting as a warden of the lands of the Marquis shall owe unto him homage and fealty, and shall swear before his peers to preserve his peace, defend his lands, uphold his lawful judgments, and neither aid nor knowingly conceal those who make war against him as so too does he to the Royarch of Bretonnia.

No oath made thereafter shall absolve a vassal of that fealty which was first lawfully sworn, save by release of the Marquis or forfeiture of the fief.

II. Summons to Arms

When the Marquis raises his banner for the defense of the Marquisate and war, every landed vassal shall answer the summons and appear at the appointed place and day with such knights, men-at-arms, archers, servants, horses, wagons, arms, and provisions as are owed according to the extent and tenure of his lands.

Every lord shall be answerable for the mustering of those who hold beneath him, and no lesser tenant shall be required to answer separately to the Marquis where his service is already rendered through his lawful lord.

No man summoned according to his tenure may send coin in place of men unless the Marquis has granted leave for scutage or other payment.

III. Defense of the Land

Should an enemy enter the Marquisate, or should rebellion, monstrous incursion, or other great peril threaten its people, the ordinary limitations upon military service shall cease for so long as the immediate danger endures.

Every vassal capable of bearing arms shall then aid in the defense of the land, and every lord shall cause his castles, fortified houses, bridges, roads, granaries, and other defensible places to be made ready.

No lord shall deny shelter within his walls to the Marquis's soldiers when necessity requires it, provided that lawful account be made for provisions taken.

IV. Castles and Fortifications

No vassal shall erect a castle, fortified tower, walled stronghold, or other place capable of resisting lawful authority without license of the Marquis.

Every licensed fortress shall remain open to the Marquis in time of war, rebellion, or grave necessity, and its lord shall neither harbor an outlaw therein nor admit an enemy of the Marquisate.

V. Counsel

Those vassals holding directly of the Marquis shall attend his court when lawfully summoned and shall render counsel concerning war, taxation, succession, disputes between great lords, and other matters touching the welfare of the Marquisate.

No man shall be punished merely because his counsel displeases the Marquis, provided that such counsel was given faithfully and without treason.

VI. Of Aid

The Marquis may demand the customary aids owed by his vassals according to ancient right and established tenure.

No extraordinary aid shall be levied upon the vassals of the Marquisate without grave necessity or the assent of those whose customary rights require their consultation, save where invasion, rebellion, famine, or like calamity permits no delay.

VII. Roads, Bridges, and Works of Defense

Every lord shall maintain those roads, bridges, watchtowers, walls, ditches, and other works entrusted to his keeping.

Where a work serves several lordships, each shall contribute men, materials, beasts, or coin according to the custom established between them.

The deliberate neglect of a work necessary for the defense of the Marquisate, after lawful warning has been given, shall constitute a breach of feudal duty and consequent punishment.

VIII. Peace of the Marquis

No vassal shall wage private war within the Marquisate without first seeking judgment before the Marquis or his appointed court.

No lord shall raid the lands of another, seize his tenants, burn his crops, obstruct his roads, spank his people, or besiege his holdings except by lawful judgment or during open rebellion.

A man attacked unlawfully shall nevertheless retain the right to defend himself, his household, and his lands.

IX. Failure of Service

A vassal who without lawful excuse refuses the summons of the Marquis, withholds the service owed by his tenure, knowingly supplies an enemy, conceals treason, or abandons a fortress committed to his defense shall be brought before the Marquis's court.

For lesser breaches, judgment may consist of fine, additional service, loss of privilege, or temporary seizure of revenues.

For grave or repeated breaches, the offending vassal may suffer forfeiture of lands and honors including stripping of knighthood.

No hereditary fief shall be permanently forfeited for breach of feudal duty without judgment before the Marquis and the assembled peers of the accused, save where the offender has openly taken arms against the Marquis.

X. Treason

Whosoever, having sworn fealty to the Marquis, knowingly takes arms against him, delivers a fortress to his enemy, conspires at his death, gives intelligence to an invading host, or joins himself to those seeking the overthrow of his lawful authority shall be guilty of high treason.

Upon lawful conviction, his lands and honors shall be forfeit, his oaths dissolved, and his person placed at the mercy of the Marquis according to the laws governing treason.

Yet neither the wife nor the children of the condemned shall be held guilty merely by blood, unless they themselves participated in his treason.

XI. Marquis's Obligation

As the vassal owes service to his lord, so does the Marquis owe protection and justice to those who hold of him.

The Marquis shall defend the lawful possession of his faithful vassals, preserve the customs and liberties granted unto them, hear their grievances, restrain unlawful violence between them, and render judgment according to the laws and customs of the Marquisate.

Should a vassal be dispossessed without lawful judgment, the Marquis shall cause his claim to be heard and, where right is proven, restore him to that which was unlawfully taken.

Thus shall fealty bind both lord and vassal: service for protection, obedience for justice, and land for faithful duty.

Of the Mustering of Men Owed by Land and Holding

I. Soldiers Owed by the Land

Every lord and other holder of lands within the Marquisate shall be bounden to find and maintain men sufficient for the defense thereof, according to the number of households lying within his fee.

For every ten inhabited households, there shall be found and maintained one good and able man-at-arms, sound of body and fit for war, furnished according to his estate with arms and armor as ordained by his liege lord

Such a man shall be kept ready throughout the year to answer the summons of his lord and, through his lord, the summons of the Marquis.

This service shall be held as a burden upon the land and not upon the person alone; and neither the death, departure, nor infirmity of the man first named shall discharge the holding thereof.

II. Finding and Sustenance of Such Men

The ten households charged together for the finding of a man-at-arms shall provide toward his sustenance according to their means and custom, whether in silver, grain, meat, cloth, fodder, or other lawful provision.

The lord of the fee shall see that every such man be furnished with good and serviceable equipment and shall answer for any want thereof at the muster.

No husbandman shall be compelled alone to bear that charge which by custom belongeth unto the ten households together, nor shall any bailiff lay the greater burden upon one household for favor of another.

III. Muster and View of Arms

Twice in every year, or more often should peril require it, the lord, steward, bailiff, constable, or other officer having authority shall cause all men owing service under this ordinance to be assembled and their arms viewed.

Every man shall come bearing the harness and weapon under which his name standeth upon the roll, together with such other equipment as by custom he is bound to possess.

If his armor be broken, wanting, or unfit for war, the same shall be amended within forty days.

If the want remain thereafter without lawful cause, the lord of the holding shall cause it to be supplied and may recover the reasonable cost thereof from those upon whom the obligation lieth.

IV. The Summons to Arms

When the Marquis raiseth his banner, every lord shall cause the men-at-arms owed from his fee to assemble beneath his own banner and shall bring them unto the place appointed within the time commanded.

Every man shall come armed, arrayed, and provisioned according to the custom of his holding.

No man owing such service shall absent himself without lawful excuse, nor shall any lord knowingly withhold from the Marquis those men whose service issueth from his lands.

V. Of the General Muster

If foreign host enter the land, if rebellion be raised against the Marquis, if the Marquisate be broken, or if such other great peril arise that the common peace may not otherwise be preserved, the Marquis may command the General Muster.

Then shall every lord raise his banner and bring forth without delay all knights, serjeants, men-at-arms, and other fighting men lawfully owing service within his fee.

Those maintained by the ten-household ordinance shall be reckoned first among the men owed and shall remain under arms until the peril be ended or they be lawfully dismissed.

VI. Census of Households

The bailiffs shall keep true rolls of all inhabited households within every village, manor, borough, and township and shall return the same unto their lord when commanded.

For every full ten households there shall be owed one soldier.

No household shall knowingly be hidden, nor two households falsely reckoned as one, nor any dwelling struck from the roll for gift, friendship, kinship, fear, or favor.

Whosoever, being charged with the keeping of such rolls, knowingly maketh false return shall answer before his lord's court and make good all service thereby withheld.

VII. Duty of Commoners

Every male child born, having attained his tenth year, shall thereafter be taught and exercised in the use of arms, that he may in due season be fit for the defense of his lord, his home, and the land.

His father, guardian, master, or household shall see that he be instructed in bow, crossbow, spear, bill, or other lawful weapon of war, according to the custom of his home and such ordinances as his lord may appoint.

From his tenth year onward he shall attend such days of practice and muster as are commanded by the liege lord and shall continue therein until age, infirmity, or other lawful cause release him from the obligation.

No boy beneath the age appointed for the levy shall by reason of this ordinance be compelled unto war; training in youth shall prepare him for service in manhood and shall not itself constitute service of arms.

Upon attaining the lawful age of levy, every able-bodied male commoner shall be liable to the Peasant Levy and when lawfully summoned shall come bearing the weapon wherein he hath been trained, together with such other arms and provisions as custom requireth.

No man shall plead ignorance of arms as excuse from the levy where he hath been bound by this ordinance to learn their use.

Thus shall every son of the commoners be bred unto husbandry in peace and made ready for the defense of the land in war.

VIII. Duty of Lords

Every lord shall answer unto the Marquis for the service issuing from the lands which he holdeth.

Where ten households owe one man-at-arms, the lord shall answer for one; where fifty owe five, he shall answer for five; where one hundred owe ten, he shall answer for ten; and so forth according to the true reckoning of his fee.

No lord shall plead the disobedience of his tenants as excuse for failing in the service which he himself oweth unto his liege.

Rather shall he distrain those who withhold their lawful portion according to the custom of his manor and judgment of his court.

IX. Of Concealment and Default

If any lord knowingly conceal the true number of households upon his lands and avoids census, dismiss men falsely from the rolls, take silver in secret for exemption from service, or otherwise diminish the number of men owed unto the Marquis, he shall make good the whole deficiency and suffer such amercement as shall be adjudged.

If he persist after warning and lawful judgment, the revenues of his fee may be seized until satisfaction be made.

And if through such willful default a castle, bridge, pass, township, or other place committed unto his keeping be lost unto the enemy, he shall answer for the same before the Marquis and his peers, upon peril of forfeiture of fee, franchise, and honour.

X. Saving of Rights

Provided always that nothing herein shall take from any lord, or other holder such liberties, exemptions, or particular customs as have been lawfully granted by charter and faithfully observed from old time.

Nevertheless, where the Marquisate itself standeth in manifest peril, no privilege shall excuse a man from such service as by his tenure and fealty he rightfully oweth.

Thus shall the strength of the land follow the wealth of the land: from every ten households, one man for its defense; from every lord, the service of his fee; and from the Marquis, the keeping and protection of all.

No lord charged with the finding of men under this ordinance shall of his own will render silver in lieu of the men owed.

Nevertheless, where the Marquis deemeth coin of greater service unto the defense of the land, he may grant unto any holder leave to discharge some part of his due or complete by payment of scutage, according to such sum as shall be assessed for every man thereby excused.

XI. Equivalences of Marshalled Forces

If a lord brings a knight to bear within his personal retinue for the muster the knight is considered equal to five common soldiers in number when reckoning for the service

No man shall be reckoned as a knight merely by reason that he possesseth horse and harness. He shall have entered knighthood and swore all vows of chivalry according to the old customs and Knight Orders of the Land, dubbed or otherwise acknowledged according to the old ways, and shall present himself with horse, arms, armour, and if need be, such attendants as properly belong unto his degree.

A knight lacking good horse, proper harness, or arms fit for service may, upon view of the marshal, be reckoned only as a common soldier until such deficiency be amended.

XII. How a Common Soldier is to be Armed

Every lord bounden to find common soldiers by reason of land or fee shall, at his own charge, arm and harness those men sufficiently for war, and shall answer for the sufficiency thereof at muster.

Every man-at-arms shall be furnished, at the least, with a good helm of iron or steel; gambeson, jack, mail, coat-of-plates, or other approved defense of the body; and one principal weapon of war, being spear, bill, bow, crossbow, sword, axe, or such other arm as the Marquis or his officers shall allow.

Those whose chief weapon is bow, crossbow, spear, or other arm not readily employed at close quarters shall further be furnished with sword, axe, mace, dagger, or other sufficient side-arm.

Shield or buckler shall be provided where proper unto the manner of service for which the man is called.

All arms and harness shall be sound, serviceable, and fit for war. No man presented with broken, rotten, greatly rusted, or otherwise insufficient gear shall be reckoned toward the service owed from the fee until the deficiency be made good.

For the lord who oweth armed men unto his liege shall furnish men fit for battle, to fight and die for the protection of his people.

The Charters of Scutage

1. #### Charters of Scutage

Any lord owing men by reason of land may make petition unto the Marquis for a Charter of Scutage, whereby a certain part, or where expressly granted the whole, of the military service issuing from his lands may be rendered in silver in lieu thereof.

The petition shall declare the lands for which such liberty is sought, the number of men otherwise owed therefrom, and such cause as the petitioner putteth forth in support thereof.

The granting of such charter shall rest wholly in the judgment and pleasure of the Marquis. No man shall have right unto such charter merely by reason of wealth, rank, former service, ancient petition, or because another hath received the like.

Every Charter of Scutage shall name the lands unto which it pertaineth, the number of men whose service may be commuted, the sum to be rendered in their stead, and such other conditions as the Marquis shall see fit to impose.

And no such charter shall release the lands from their burden of military service, but shall stand only as the Marquis's leave that the manner of rendering that service be altered.

2. #### Revocation

Every Charter of Scutage shall be held at the pleasure of the Marquis and may be diminished, suspended, or wholly revoked whenever the defense or necessity of the Marquisate so requireth.

No length of possession, succession of heirs, repeated acceptance of payment, or former sufferance shall turn such charter into an irrevocable right.

Upon lawful notice of its revocation, the holder shall thereafter find the full number of men owing from his lands, according to this ordinance, notwithstanding any scutage formerly paid.

Nor shall compensation be owed for the loss of such liberty, save where the Marquis himself hath expressly covenanted otherwise under seal.

3. #### Scutage in Time of Peril

No Charter of Scutage shall bind the Marquis during invasion, rebellion, siege, or other great peril.

Upon proclamation of the Great Muster, every Charter of Scutage shall be deemed suspended for the duration thereof unless the Marquis expressly command otherwise.

Then shall every holder find the full number of men owed from his lands and send them armed and arrayed according to this ordinance, notwithstanding any charter, payment, custom, or former exemption to the contrary.

4. #### Personal Service

The payment of scutage shall not excuse any lord from appearing in his own person where his homage, tenure, or dignity requireth personal service, unless the Marquis expressly release him therefrom.

Thus a lord may by charter commute the service of those men issuing from his lands whilst remaining himself bound to answer the banner of his liege.

5. #### Scutage Rendered Without Leave

Any holder who withholdeth a man-at-arms lawfully owed and offereth coin without leave or charter shall be held not to have rendered his service, notwithstanding that such silver be tendered unto the treasury.

And any officer who, without warrant of the Marquis, taketh coin for the excusing of men from the array shall restore twice the sum received and suffer such further amercement as the Marquis's court shall adjudge.

For scutage is a liberty granted and not a right possessed; and that which the Marquis granteth for the good of the land may, for the good of the land, be called again unto his hand.

Nobility, Knighthood, and the Holding of Land

1. ### Those Who May Hold Land

No person shall hold a landed fee in his own right within the Marquisate unless he be lawfully received into knighthood.

Noble birth without knighthood shall give right of inheritance, but not full possession of the fee.

Knighthood without nobility shall not be known in law.

Thus shall landed lordship require nobility by blood or lawful grant, and thereafter knighthood duly received.

II. Of Those Who May Receive Knighthood

No person of common estate shall be dubbed, received, proclaimed, or otherwise admitted unto the sacred dignity of knighthood.

Knighthood shall belong unto the nobility alone.

Before any man be dubbed knight, his noble estate shall first be known and acknowledged according to the laws and customs of the Marquisate. His lineage and pedigree must be confirmed by historian and may originate from foreign lands.

Where his nobility standeth doubtful, the dubbing shall be stayed until his descent or lawful grant of nobility be proved before competent authority.

No lord, howsoever great his estate, shall knowingly make knight of a common man.

III. Of Unlawful Dubbing

If any lord knowingly dub a commoner knight before that man hath lawfully entered the noble estate, the dubbing shall be void and of no force in law.

The person so dubbed shall acquire thereby neither noble estate, knightly privilege, precedence, right to bear knightly style, nor capacity to hold land.

The lord who knowingly performed such unlawful dubbing shall answer before the proper court for contempt of the ordinance and suffer such amercement or other judgment as befitteth his rank.

A commoner who knowingly claimeth knightly dignity by virtue of an unlawful dubbing shall likewise answer for false assumption of dignity.

IV. Of Ennoblement Before Knighthood

A person born of common estate may nevertheless be raised unto nobility by the Marquis according to lawful custom.

Such ennoblement shall precede knighthood.

Once letters of nobility have been lawfully granted and proclaimed, the person so ennobled shall thereafter possess the same capacity to seek and receive knighthood as another nobleman, subject to the customary requirements thereof.

No act shall be presumed to confer all three dignities at once unless the Marquis expressly declare the same under his seal.

V. Of Noble Birth

A person shall be accounted noble where he is lawfully born of a house acknowledged as noble or hath himself been raised unto noble estate by lawful grant of the Marquis.

Neither wealth, command of soldiers, possession of arms, marriage unto nobility, learned office, service in war, nor long exercise of authority shall of itself make a man noble.

Nor shall any commoner become noble merely because men address him as lord, knight, or other title belonging unto a higher estate.

VI. Of the Sons of Noble Houses

The sons of noble houses shall be accounted noble by birth according to the laws of descent, but shall not thereby be accounted knights.

They may serve their in capacity befitting their station until they begin their errand at which time they may be dubbed a knight by a lord in good standing.

No nobleman shall style himself “Sir”, claim the privileges peculiar unto knighthood, or exercise an office expressly reserved unto knights merely because he is heir unto a noble house.

VII. Proof Required Before Dubbing

Before a man be received into knighthood, the lord performing the dubbing, or his appointed herald or officer, shall be satisfied of the candidate's noble estate.

Proof may be made by known descent, heraldic roll, letters of nobility, pedigree, testimony of reputable nobles, or judgment of a competent Court.

Where fraud is afterward discovered, the matter shall be brought before the Marquis or his proper officers.

VIII. False Claim to Knighthood

Whosoever knowingly assumeth the style, arms, privileges, or dignity of knight without lawful dubbing shall be guilty of false knighthood.

Likewise shall any commoner who falsely claimeth noble descent for the purpose of obtaining knighthood answer for the same.

Where forged pedigree, seal, letters patent, or heraldic record hath been employed, the offender shall suffer the further penalties appointed for falsification of charters and seals.

IX. Of Knighthood and Landed Possession

No nobleman, though lawfully born, shall enter into full possession of a landed fee until he hath received knighthood.

Where land descendeth unto a noble heir not yet knighted, his inheritance shall be preserved but remain in wardship according to law.

Upon receiving knighthood and performing the homage and fealty owed for the fee, he shall be admitted unto possession.

For nobility maketh a man capable of the lance; the lance maketh him capable of lordship; and lordship bindeth him unto the service of the land and honor in the field.

X. Of the Prerogative of the Marquis

The power to raise a common man unto noble estate shall belong unto the Marquis, as he and he alone acts with the authority granted by the Royarch of Bretonnia. No Baron, Count, Earl, or other lesser lord may by his own authority ennoble a commoner. At his pleasure the Marquis may bestow a Writ of Blood and grant a commoner all the rights and privileges of a noble and at the Marquis’ discretion this right may be passed down to his sons in perpetuity unless revoked.

A lesser lord may commend a worthy man unto the Marquis and petition for his advancement, but until lawful Writ of Blood and Dignity be granted, the man shall remain of common estate.

Once ennobled, however, he may thereafter begin his errand to be dubbed knight by such person as possesseth lawful authority to confer knighthood.

Any found guilty of attempting to ennoble a commoner will share the same fate as the commoner as judged by the Marquis himself.

XI. Arms Befitting the Dignity of a Knight

No knight within the Marquisate shall bear or employ in battle bow, crossbow, hand-gonne, sling, or other weapon whose chief purpose is to strike an enemy from afar, such arms being held contrary unto the manner and dignity of knightly combat.

A knight shall enter righteous war by sword, lance, spear, mace, axe, or other knightly weapon wielded by his own hand at close quarters, whether he fight mounted or upon foot.

Nothing herein shall forbid a knight from commanding archers, crossbowmen, gunners, or other soldiers armed with weapons of distance, for the dishonour lieth not in their lawful employment, but in the knight himself taking up such arms in place of those proper unto his dignity.

Nor shall the casting of a broken weapon in extremity, or other act done for the immediate preservation of life, be accounted a breach of this ordinance.

Whosoever knowingly forsaketh the arms of his digniy and maketh habitual use of weapons of distance shall answer before his peers for conduct unbecoming of knighthood, and may suffer censure, loss of privilege, or such other judgment as knightly custom requireth.

For the knight is bounden to meet his foe beneath the reach of lance and sword, and shall not seek his honour from afar. He is to be an example of war to the common man and under the gaze of the gods he must be virtuous in combat and by skill and strength alone may he be victor.

XII. The Order of Estates

Thus shall the order of dignity be maintained within the Marquisate:

The nobleman may earn knighthood.
The knight may hold landed lordship.
And the landed lord shall answer for the service of his fee.

None shall take the dignity of the estate above him without lawful advancement, and no dignity lawfully granted shall release a man from the duties thereby assumed.

A noble may only be granted land provided he can populate the land with ten households.

Charter for the Keeping of Blackpowder Weapons

I. Charters for the Keeping of Blackpowder Weapons

No person shall petition for a Charter of Ordinance save one who lawfully holdeth the dignity and estate of knighthood within the Marquisate.

A knight, banneret, lord of a manor, or other person or body of lesser dignity may be strictly prohibited from employing such weapons by his liege lord.

2. ### Petition

Any Baron, Count, or Earl desiring leave to possess guns shall make petition unto the Marquis and therein declare:

the number and manner of guns desired;

the castle, fortress, estate, or other place wherein they shall ordinarily be kept;

and the cause for which such ordnance is sought.

The Marquis may thereupon grant the petition wholly, grant it only in part, impose such conditions as he deemeth needful, or refuse it altogether.

The right to petition shall not be construed as a right to possess.

No Baron, Count, or Earl shall claim entitlement unto ordnance merely by reason of his rank, nor because another noble of like or lesser dignity hath received such privilege.

III. Of the Particular Grant

Every Charter of Ordnance shall name both the holder and the fee unto which the privilege pertaineth.

No general words of privilege shall be taken to grant more than is expressly written therein.

Thus a charter for cannon shall not grant hand-guns; a charter for hand-guns shall not grant cannons or other weapons

IV. Of Lesser Lords and Knights

No knight, banneret, lord of manor, or other person beneath baronial dignity shall privately possess a gun by reason that his liege possesseth a Charter of Ordinance.

Nevertheless, such persons may employ blackpowder weapons of their lord while lawfully serving within his household, garrison, army, or company, provided that the weapons remain the property and under the authority of the chartered lord.

Those elevated unto knighthood are expressly prohibited from wielding such dishonorable weapons at the risk of dishonor.

Thus may a knight command gunners without himself possessing the privilege of ordnance, and a soldier may bear hand-gun in his lord's service without acquiring any right to keep the same as his own.

V. Nature of the Privilege

A Charter of Ordnance shall be accounted a special grace of the Marquis and no incident of nobility.

It shall not pass merely with blood, dignity, inheritance, or succession unless the charter expressly provideth for such continuance.

The Marquis may amend, diminish, suspend, or revoke the charter at his pleasure where the peace or defense of the Marquisate so requireth.

Upon revocation, the holder shall surrender or otherwise dispose of the ordnance according to lawful command.

Neither ancient possession, repeated renewal, faithful service, nor succession of heirs shall make permanent that which was first bestowed by grace.

For the keeping of gonne and powder belongeth not unto nobility by right, but unto those great lords whom the Marquis judgeth worthy to be entrusted with such engines of war.

Fabricating, Forging, and Making of Blackpowder weapons

I. Making of Blackpowder Weapons

No smith, founder, armourer, artificer, guild, lord, merchant, or other person whatsoever shall found, forge, bore, fashion, assemble, or otherwise make any cannon, bombard, hand-gun, arquebus, or other weapon made to cast shot by black powder, save under lawful warrant of the Marquis.

Nor shall any man cause such weapons to be made secretly or by another in his stead.

Whosoever causeth unlawful ordnance to be made shall answer for the offense as though he had fashioned the same with his own hands.

Blackpowder weapons will strictly follow a quality as agreed by master artificers of the guilds and other

II. Blackpowder Charter

The Marquis may grant unto such master founders, smiths, artificers, workshops, or foundries as he deemeth trustworthy a Blackpowder Charter, whereby they may lawfully make such ordnance as is permitted therein.

Every such warrant shall declare:

the person, guild, or workshop unto whom it is granted;

the place wherein the work may be undertaken;

the manner of blackpowder weapons which may be made;

and such other conditions concerning their manufacture as the Marquis shall see fit to impose.

No Blackpowder Charter shall be held a perpetual liberty.

It may be amended, suspended, or revoked at the pleasure of the Marquis, and no length of practice shall turn the same into right or custom.

III. Charters of Ordnance

A Charter of Ordinance granteth leave to keep; it granteth not leave to make.

Thus no Baron, Count, or Earl possessing lawful Charter of Ordnance may establish a foundry, employ craftsmen for the making of blackpowder weapons, or cause new pieces to be fashioned upon his lands unless separate warrant hath been granted therefor.

Neither shall possession of forge, furnace, mine, smithy, watermill, foundry, or other work suitable to the making of ordnance enlarge the privilege contained within his charter.

IV. Of Guns Made for Chartered Lords

A master holding lawful Blackpowder Charter may make weapons for a Baron, Count, or Earl possessing a Charter of Ordnance, provided that the weapon be of a manner which that lord is lawfully permitted to possess.

Before undertaking such work, the master shall have sight of the lord's charter or lawful warrant proceeding therefrom.

V. Of the Marquis's Ordnance

The Marquis may command any warranted foundry within his lands to make ordnance for his arsenals, castles, armies, or other service, reasonable payment being rendered according to agreement, custom, or lawful assessment.

Ordnance made upon the Marquis's command shall be marked and entered upon the rolls of his Master of Ordnance before it be issued unto fortress, captain, ship, or company.

No weapon belonging unto the Marquis shall be sold, pledged, bestowed, melted, or otherwise disposed of without lawful warrant.

VI. Marks and Proof

Every weapon lawfully made within the Marquisate shall bear the mark of its maker and such guild mark or seal or device of the Marquis's ordnance as shall be ordained.

Before delivery, every cannon, bombard, or other great gonne shall be proved.

No piece failing such proof shall be delivered for war.

The maker shall amend, recast, or destroy the faulty piece according to the judgment of the officer overseeing the proof.

No man shall knowingly remove, alter, counterfeit, or conceal the lawful marks borne upon a gonne.

VII. Foreign Blackpowder Weapons

No blackpowder weapons made beyond the Marquisate shall be brought within its bounds without declaration unto the officers of the Marquis.

A Baron, Count, or Earl possessing Charter of Ordnance may petition for leave to purchase ordnance from foreign lands, but no foreign purchase shall be made merely by virtue of the charter unless the charter expressly granteth such liberty.

All foreign pieces lawfully brought within the Marquisate shall be viewed, proved, marked, and entered upon the rolls before they may be employed unless extreme need caused by urgency.

VIII. Of Unlawful Foundries

Where any secret furnace, workshop, forge, or foundry be discovered wherein blackpowder weapons are unlawfully made, the officers of the Marquis may seize the weapons, tools, moulds, and materials employed therein according to lawful judgment.

The master thereof shall answer before the Court.

Where it be shown that such manufacture arose from ignorance or lesser disobedience, the offender may suffer forfeiture and amercement.

But where weapons have been secretly made in number for rebellion, treason, or the arming of the Marquis's enemies, the makers, patrons, and knowing accomplices shall answer according to the laws governing those greater offenses.

IX. Of the Master's Responsibility

The master whose mark standeth upon a gonne shall answer for the honesty of its making.

If through willful use of false metal, concealment of grave defect, or other knowing deceit a piece bursteth and thereby bringeth death or grievous hurt unto those lawfully employing it, the master shall answer before the Court for the harm occasioned by his fraud.

But no master shall be held answerable merely because a sound piece afterward faileth through age, misuse, neglect, overcharging, enemy stroke, or other cause beyond his workmanship.

X. Of the Marquis's Prerogative

The fabrication of blackpowder weapons shall remain an especial privilege proceeding from the Marquis.

No lord shall claim the art by tenure; no guild shall claim monopoly by custom; no town shall claim it by liberty; and no craftsman shall claim it merely because his fathers practiced the same.

Lawful Duels and the Settlement of Quarrels

Be it known unto all men, present and to come, that whereas quarrels of honour, accusation, debt, insult, injury, and other grievances oft arise between men, and whereas such quarrels, if left ungoverned, breed murder, feud, and disturbance of the Marquis's peace, it is ordained that certain disputes may be settled by lawful duel according to the customs hereafter written.

I. Of the Lawfulness of the Duel

A duel freely undertaken according to this ordinance shall not be accounted murder, assault, affray, or breach of the Marquis's peace.

No man shall be punished merely for giving or accepting lawful challenge, nor for wounds honestly dealt in the course thereof.

If death befall either combatant in a duel lawfully begun and lawfully fought, the survivor shall not for that cause be held guilty of homicide.

Yet no duel shall be deemed lawful unless the conditions herein ordained have been observed.

II. Of Causes for Challenge

A man may offer challenge where there standeth between him and another a grave quarrel touching honour, accusation, debt, broken oath, insult, injury, disputed possession, or other matter for which satisfaction hath been demanded and refused.

No man shall challenge another for sport alone, for drunken boasting, for wagering of coin, or for mere delight in bloodshed.

Nor shall challenge excuse an offense committed against the Marquis, the peace of the realm, or the common good.

Treason, murder, rape, robbery, arson, rebellion, and other pleas belonging unto the high justice of the Marquis shall not be extinguished by private duel.

III. Of Challenge and Acceptance

The challenge shall be plainly spoken before witnesses or delivered in writing under the challenger's hand or seal.

The cause of quarrel shall be declared, so that no man be drawn into hazard of his life without knowing the grievance laid against him.

The challenged may accept, refuse, or seek judgment before the proper court.

Refusal of challenge shall not of itself constitute confession of guilt, nor shall any man be compelled by force to accept a private duel where no law, oath, or particular custom bindeth him thereto.

Once challenge hath been given and accepted before witnesses, both parties shall be bound to keep the appointed place, day, and conditions unless they be reconciled beforehand.

IV. Of the Place and Witnesses

No lawful duel shall be fought secretly.

There shall be present no fewer than two witnesses, one chosen by each combatant, who shall attest the challenge, the weapons agreed upon, and the manner in which the duel was concluded.

Where the quarrel concerneth men of noble estate, land, inheritance, or other matter of consequence, a herald, knight, magistrate, bailiff, or other lawful officer should be called to witness the combat where reasonably possible.

No duel shall knowingly be fought within church, sanctuary, marketplace during market, court while sitting, or other place specially protected by the Marquis's peace.

V. Lawful Weapons

All lawful duels shall be fought hand to hand and at close quarters.

The proper weapon of duel shall be the sword, whether arming sword, longsword, great sword, falchion, sabre, estoc, or other sword commonly borne within the Marquisate and agreed upon by the combatants.

The parties shall, so far as reasonably may be done, meet with weapons of like kind and comparable condition.

Shield, buckler, cloak, or dagger may be permitted where both parties agree before the combat and the same is witnessed.

No man shall secretly bear a second weapon not agreed upon beforehand.

VI. Of Unlawful Arms

No bow, crossbow, sling, firearm, hand-gun, thrown spear, javelin, dart, or other weapon whose chief purpose is to strike from afar shall be employed in lawful duel as they are cowardly and without grace.

Neither combatant shall knowingly withdraw beyond the appointed ground for the purpose of attacking his adversary from afar.

No poison shall be laid upon a weapon.

No trap, concealed engine, accomplice, beast trained for war, or other device shall be employed to strike an adversary without the hand of the combatant himself.

No charm, spell, enchanted missile, summoned creature, or other supernatural art shall be employed unless a particular law expressly provideth otherwise.

The judgment of the duel shall lie in courage and mastery of arms at hand, and not in the slaying of a man from beyond the reach of his sword.

The combatants may fight in armour or without it according to the conditions agreed when challenge is accepted.

Where armour is permitted, each may bear any defensive equipment proper unto his estate.

Neither party shall knowingly conceal beneath his clothing any armor or defense forbidden by the agreed conditions.

If no condition concerning harness hath been agreed, each combatant may wear such armour as he possesseth.

VIII. Of the Ending of the Duel

Before swords are crossed, the parties shall declare whether the duel be unto submission or unto death.

A duel unto submission shall cease when one combatant yieldeth himself plainly by word or sign, is rendered unable to continue, or is disarmed and refuseth further contest.

Once surrender hath plainly been given, no further blow shall lawfully be struck.

He who knowingly slayeth an adversary after lawful surrender shall not claim the protection of the duel and may answer for murder according to law.

A duel declared unto death shall continue until one combatant yieldeth, is unable to continue, or is slain.

No man shall be compelled to slay an adversary who hath yielded merely because the duel was declared unto death.

IX. Of the Satisfaction of the Quarrel

When a lawful duel hath been concluded, the quarrel for which it was undertaken shall be held answered and satisfied between the combatants.

Neither party nor their households shall thereafter renew the same quarrel by challenge, vengeance, ambush, or feud.

Where land, coin, goods, or some particular satisfaction formed the subject of the agreement preceding the duel, the result shall have such force as was agreed and witnessed beforehand.

But no duel between private men shall deprive a third person of his lawful rights, nor shall it bind the Marquis in matters touching his revenues, justice, or authority.

X. Of False and Unlawful Duels

If men fight without witnesses, employ forbidden weapons, conceal unlawful advantages, bring accomplices into the combat, continue after surrender, or otherwise knowingly break the conditions under which challenge was accepted, the protection of this ordinance shall be lost.

The offender may thereafter answer for the wounds or death caused by him as though the lawful privilege of duel had not protected those acts.

XI. Of the Keeping of the Marquis's Peace

Nothing herein shall be taken as license for men to draw swords whenever anger moveth them.

A sudden affray in tavern, street, hall, camp, or market remaineth an affray notwithstanding that one man afterward nameth it duel.

Challenge must precede combat, acceptance must precede the drawing of swords, and witnesses must stand to the covenant between them.

Thus shall honour have its remedy without every quarrel becoming feud, and the sword settle that which disputing tongues cannot, whilst the peace and justice of the Marquis remain undiminished.

entries.title: Reign of Ramnulf the Proud, 2431
entries.body:
“..We shall inspire our lessers and show the villains the might of our rage, ride now, knights of Sontrailles!..”

- Words of Marquis Ramnulf de Naizon before the battle of Moslac Plains, as recorded by historian Rolin of Sontrailles, 2435

The crusade continued for the greenskins were without and new warlords rose up to challenge the knights who believed truly in the divine inspiration of the Lady. Ramnulf did not have time to grieve his friend’s death for the orcs threw themselves at the walls of Sontrailles and he needed to lead its defense. Three times they attacked and were thus repulsed three times before they broke. On the fourth day Ramnulf gathered his host and set forth upon a campaign against the marauding greenskin hordes. Within weeks days, all lands within five leagues were purged of the orcish blight, and before a fortnight had passed, the severed heads of four orc warlords stood impaled upon the ramparts of Sontrailles. Early in his reign he played the role of savior, those he saved often found themselves graciously compelled to offer a sum of gold, enough to fuel his war and keep his knights well equipped, lest their lands be left vulnerable once more. A man of simple stratagem, the new marquis held in utter contempt the base and craven arts of ambush and flanking, deeming them unworthy of a true knight. Even in this foreign land, his noble disdain remained untempered, for he looked upon his neighbors and their mercenary rabble as naught but feeble, undisciplined swine of common stock. Nevertheless, his vows of chivalry compelled him to lend his lance and shield to those in need, standing against all evil. Soon in time the princes would come to the same conclusion, no single host could hope to stand alone against the relentless tide of the green menace. Only through a series of alliances might they endure. And so, wherever the greenskins went they found themselves facing a united force. Ramnulf led his knights to aid neighboring settlements, from the River Limnalia in the west to the Skull River in the east. Though his demeanor outside of battle was often haughty, on the battlefield, he fought alongside the other Border Princes as brothers. The green menace would find no quarter in the lands under his watch, for the marquis and his knights patrolled far and wide, and no orc, troll, or marauding goblin dared linger where Bretonnian arms and honor held sway. The historian Rolin wrote of the battle,

“ As the orks approached they began throwing spears towards our lines and so the battle began. The Marquis’ regiment bore the first shock, a weighty one. Those orks proud and in great heart, came down upon them fiercely, butting their misshapen weapons into them with all the force of their chests and shoulders as though they were wild boars. And they were knit so tightly together so their ranks would not easily be broken and the men at arms gave ground. The knight errants and bachelors in the wings earned great honor that day as they rode around and smashed into their flanks and the orks became hard pressed. They were impaled upon stout lances of Virtuous Steel and in that moment the orks shrank from our valour.”

When the greenskins’ advance was blunted and their remnants driven back toward the Badlands for a time, Ramnulf turned his full attention to the shaping of what had been won. No longer content with mere survival, he devoted himself to the expansion and fortification of the settlement, that it might endure against all foes yet to come. Under his watchful eye, Sontrailles grew beyond its humble origins, its foundations strengthened against both mortal enemies and the lingering touch of the supernatural. Within Aedric’s Rest, a shrine to the Lady was solemnly consecrated, its halls graced by a devoted congregation of Grail Monks, men drawn from the ranks of pious camp followers who had endured the march from Bretonnia and the siege. As the city expanded westward, its walls were reinforced and new districts raised, each built with the comforts and order of civilization in mind. At first, necessity alone guided this growth, blacksmiths’ forges roared to life, ensuring that knights and their retainers were well armed and armored. Over time homes and shops spread across the rolling hills, and with them came a sense of permanence and stability. What had once been little more than a frontier castle was transformed into a thriving city.

Sontrailles soon became one of a handful strongholds capable of withstanding the ceaseless depredations of marauding greenskin warbands, rampaging warherds, and the ever present menace of the undead. Many fiefs within leagues were founded but most did not survive. Because of this, desperate souls arrived in droves, swelling the city’s population. Skilled craftsmen, masons, blacksmiths, and artisans of every kind, found no shortage of labor as they fortified the city and armed its defenders. Those without a trade were not turned away, for there was always need of strong hands. Some labored in the endless works of construction, while others were graciously allowed to work plots of land under the patronage of newly landed knights, binding them to the realm. Those skilled artisans who had contributed most heavily to Sontrailles were duly rewarded. Foremost among them was Giefferen, a master smith whose family had perfected their craft over generations, producing steel of exceptional purity and strength. This metal, later known as “Virtuous Steel,” earned Giefferen and his line the rights and privileges of nobility. Thus elevated, the Durocher family was granted residence within the castle itself and a manor in the surrounding hills, holdings they retain to this day.

Seeing this rapid growth, Ramnulf established a feudal order modeled upon the fair customs of Bretonnia. All who sought shelter within Sontrailles were required to pledge fealty and labor in exchange for protection. Those unwilling to accept such bonds were left with a simple choice to take up arms upon the front lines and pray to whatever gods might listen, or to depart and fend for themselves beyond the walls. Bretonnian law was formally enacted, reinforcing hierarchy, chivalry, and duty, while outlawing the use of black powder weapons, that knightly valor might remain untainted. Most refugees became peasants beneath the city’s landed lords, while the military was organized in Bretonnian fashion. Men-at-arms guarded toll roads and trade routes vital to the city’s prosperity, and all able bodied men, regardless of station, were drilled to defend the high walls of Sontrailles should the need arise. Despite the dangers that surrounded him, Ramnulf would not sully his cause by hiring mercenaries, holding such practices in contempt. His faith rested instead in those sworn to chivalry, and the steady stream of refugees, properly trained, proved a boon rather than a burden. Justice itself he oversaw personally, holding court to enforce the law and preserve order.

As Sontrailles rose in power, envoys from other Border Princes and from nearby Dwarf holds arrived seeking favorable trade and alliance, recognizing in the city a bastion of stability and martial strength. When Ramnulf’s son, Jean, came of age, he entrusted him with the study of governance and diplomacy, setting him to hold court in his stead under the guidance of his most trusted advisors, that he might learn the delicate arts that had come to define his father’s rule.
Knights answering the call to war found within Sontrailles a place of refuge and respite, where warm food and ample provisions were freely given. In return, many swore oaths of service to the marquis and took up residence within his domain. The damsels who often accompanied these knights were lodged according to their high station, yet none chose to remain within the chapel of the Lady, despite the grace that surely imbued its walls. Instead, they moved onward at the call of the Royarch, lending their aid to the wider crusade and to Charlen’s wars yet they lent their blessed favors to worthy knights before their departure. For that same cause Ramnulf sent his younger brother, Vortigern, who led a company of knights and men-at-arms to fight beside the crusaders. In this way did Sontrailles give of its strength beyond its own borders. Fate would decree that the brothers should never look upon one another again in life, though their deeds would endure together in memory.

Twenty years into Ramnulf’s reign, the greenskins had been driven deep into the Badlands by the relentless advance of the knights and their allies. Their presence within the Border Princes waned at last, and where once they had surged in endless hordes, they now lingered only as scattered remnants, no longer the great threat of former years. With this reprieve hard won, the marquis turned his gaze to other matters, for the borderlands were never truly at peace.
Though the orcs were beaten for a time, the land yet crawled with perils uncounted, beastmen warherds stalking the wilds, chaos cults festering in secret, skaven ambushing peasants and disappearing just as quickly, undead haunting nearby cursed lands, and, from time to time, swift and cruel raids by the dark elves. Above all lingered the long shadow of the lich’s curse, a blight upon the land that refused to fade. Whenever Morrslieb waxed full in the heavens, its sickly green light washing across fields and forest alike, the dead would stir once more. Corpses clawed their way free of the cold earth, heedless of grave or sanctified ground. Even within the fortified walls of Sontrailles, the restless dead rose anew, hollow eyes burning with pallid witchfire. Time and again, the living were forced to take up arms against these abominations, hewing them down before they could retake the land. This unending cycle had to end.

Aware of the ancient catacombs and barrows hidden beneath the Geistenmund Hills, Ramnulf dispatched carefully chosen men from his personal retinue, together with learned clergy steeped in the sacred rites of purification, to scour the depths beneath the city itself. Their charge was clear to locate these forgotten crypts, long sealed in shadow, and to cleanse them of any lingering necromantic taint, perhaps even to shatter the lich’s curse once and for all.
Beyond this, his gaze turned northward to the greater Geistenmund Hills. Their proximity to Sontrailles and promise of expansion were enticing. His advisors spoke of fertile lands in the valley between the hills that might yet be reclaimed once the necromantic corruption was burned away, yet Ramnulf knew that such a venture would be easily won.

There were rumors that a vampiric lord who had ruled these hills since before the Sun King cast the necromancers into the Borderlands. Some claimed the dark knights who once rode beside the lich had been vampires themselves, and if such beings yet served a greater master, they would prove weapons of dreadful potency in the wars to come.
Ramnulf understood the gravity of his situation. To uproot such an evil would possibly require more forces then he had at hand yet there could be no room for doubt, for the valleys were vital to the future of Sontrailles. The land could not be left to fester beneath such corruption. To claim it would mean more than expansion; it would be the purging of an ancient wound and the safeguarding of the people entrusted to him. In preparation, Ramnulf quietly ensured the city’s garrison was provisioned to withstand a long siege, should the greenskins strike while he was abroad on campaign.

Mousillon was cursed and forever stalked by the terrors of the night and was Ramnulf’s birthplace. Such horrors had long fed upon its fear and despair, and he was no stranger to their insidious ability to rot the hearts and minds of men. For this reason, he cloaked his intentions in secrecy. Only his son, Jean, and a handful of his most trusted companions, those of proven loyalty were made privy to the true scope of his designs. His ambitions were too great, his enemies too powerful, to risk even a single whisper of betrayal. Beyond the walls of Sontrailles lay a realm rife with foes both living and dead, many of whom would sell any secret for a pittance of coin. Thus did Ramnulf prepare in silence, intending to strike when the hour was right, and to scour the night terrors and their vile masters from the land at last.

That war against the darkness, however, would not come to pass in his lifetime.
While holding court, the marquis was suddenly struck by a violent illness. Weeping ulcers bloomed upon his flesh, and he was seized by fits of vomiting foaming bile. Within days, Ramnulf was dead. Not long after, tragedy struck again. During a hunting expedition, Jean was slain by a crossbow bolt driven clean through his head, perishing alongside several of his father’s most trusted advisors. Though the marksmen were skilled, none escaped. They were captured and they would confess that the attack had been carried out under the direct orders of the Prince of Valendra.

With no surviving heirs, Ramnulf’s brother, Vortigern, ascended to the title of marquis a mere fortnight later, in the year 2463. Thus did Ramnulf forge a legacy, recorded by the historians of Sontrailles as the one who cemented the martial renown among their neighbors.

entries.title: Reign of Vortigern the Blessed
entries.body:
“..May the Lady guide us in battle so that we might cast aside the shadow with her light..”
-Words of Marquis Votigern de Naizon before the crusade north, as recorded by Heliot of Sontrailles, in the year 2479

By the time Vortigern reclaimed his brother’s seat, he had neared his sixtieth year, yet he remained a man of formidable vigor. It was said that he had found the Grail deep within the Badlands, supping from it only after a lifetime spent in the Lady’s pursuit. Soon after taking his brother’s empty throne, Vortigern mustered a host and rode forth to deliver swift justice upon the Prince of Valendra. The usurper’s mercenaries, poorly paid and unmotivated, surrendered quickly when offered safe passage in exchange for their master. The prince, feigning honor, offered a duel, which Vortigern accepted without hesitation. The prince’s demeanor changed and at once began trying to back out of the duel. With a swift flick of Vortigern’s wrist the prince’s head was severed before the man could scream his cries for mercy. But the prince's followers began proclaiming that the slain man was no prince, but a mercenary, paid most handsomely to fight in his stead. The true prince had fled, forsaking his people to their fate, and by the time the ruse was uncovered, he had a few hours head start. He was found days later, skulking near the treacherous Winter’s Teeth Pass, where he was seized, judged, and put to the sword. Word spread that whispers had reached the ears of the doomed prince rumors that the Marquis of Sontrailles sought to expand his power and subjugate his neighbors. Whether truth or falsehood, this fear had driven him to folly. Nor was he alone in his dread. Throughout the Border Princes, ambition and suspicion festered, old grievances rekindling into open war. Petty lords, long accustomed to strife, turned upon one another, their fractious alliances splintering, their feuds stoked by little more than a murmur of discontent. Some honored their oaths and held to their bonds, yet in prudence, refrained from raising their weapons in the struggle. As the land descended into chaos, an even graver peril loomed.
